The Story of Misinterpretation

I bow to Lord Jina, in whose five auspicious events — conception, birth, austerity, knowledge, and nirvana — the gods of heaven came and offered great worship and devotion, and I write a story about misinterpretation — about taking the wrong meaning.

Vasupal was king of Ayodhya. His queen was Vasumati. They had an intelligent son named Vasumitra. Vasupal entrusted his son's education to a learned scholar named Garg and launched an attack on King Veerdatt of Ujjain, because Veerdatt always insulted Vasupal and gave trouble to his subjects.

Vasupal came to Ujjain and besieged the city for some days. During this time, he sent a letter to Ayodhya regarding state administration. In it, about his son, he wrote:

'Putrodhyaapayitavyosau vasumitroatisaadaram |
Shaalibhaktamasispriktam sarpiryaktam dinam prati ||
Gargopaadhyayakasyochchai rdeeyate bhojanaaya cha |'

The meaning is: 'Arrange well for Vasumitra's education, let there be no fault, and let the teacher Garg have no trouble with food — give him ghee, rice, milk-rice, etc. daily.'

The letter arrived. The reader read it as it was. But in the verse, there is a word 'masispriktam' (मसिस्पृक्तं). In interpreting this word, he made a mistake. He understood it as an adjective of 'shaalibhaktam' (rice) and gave the meaning: 'Give the teacher rice mixed with ink to eat.' And so it was done.

The word 'masisprikt' in the verse — the author's intention is not clear. But it is used in such a place that it cannot be an adjective of 'shaalibhakt' without violating the meter. Scholar Bakhtavarmal, who composed the verse-language of the Aradhana Katha Kosh, renders these verses as:

'Sutavasumitrapadhaiyonitt, gargnaampaathakajeepavitt |
Taakobhojanatangudheev, likhanhetamasideevasadeev ||'

Scholar Bakhtavarmal has interpreted 'masisprikt' as 'give the teacher ink for writing.' He may have done this somehow, but that word does not have the power to support this meaning. And if the author too intended this meaning, then it must be said that his compositional skill was very weak.

Our belief is not based only on this verse and a half, but throughout this large work, wherever such misinterpretations occur, they show a lack of precision in language. The reader who took 'masispriktam' as 'mixed with ink' rather than 'touched with ink' (referring to writing materials) caused the teacher to be fed rice mixed with ink — a grave error born of misinterpretation.

This story teaches the critical importance of correct interpretation. A single misunderstood word can lead to absurd and harmful results. The reader who interpreted 'masispriktam' incorrectly caused the teacher to be fed ink-mixed rice instead of providing him with writing materials. The wise should be very careful in interpreting instructions, especially when the meaning is unclear. When in doubt, one should seek clarification rather than act on a potentially wrong interpretation.
